🕯️ Impure Tevel — why untithed impure produce may never be used for light, even on a weekday
🌿 Balsam and the Poor — Ein Gedi's balsam pickers and the ḥilazon trappers of the north

overview.title: 📖 Overview: From Lamp Oil to Sukkah Roofing
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 26a–26b
overview.hebrewSource: אֵין מַדְלִיקִין בְּטֶבֶל טָמֵא בַּחוֹל, וְאֵין צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר בְּשַׁבָּת
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The Gemara continues the second chapter's list of forbidden Shabbat-lamp fuels, first pinning down why tar is banned and then asking why impure untithed produce (tevel) may not be used for light even on a weekday. A cautionary tale about a mother-in-law's cruel trick with balsam oil leads into a discussion of who actually gathered balsam and the sky-blue ḥilazon dye. The daf then works through a Tosefta of five tannaim disputing exactly which oils are fit for the Shabbat lamp, with Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri objecting that people in Babylonia, Media, Alexandria, and Cappadocia have no choice but local oils. The sugya closes by pivoting to a related material question: whether cloth made from tree products (other than linen) and swatches of three-by-three fingerbreadths can become ritually impure with tzaraat.

slides.title: 🔥 Why No Tar? One Reason or Two?
slides.subtitle: The Gemara pins down the Mishna's rationale

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Let the Master simply say tar is banned because it is volatile עָף and might catch fire!

lines.speaker: Answer
lines.text: He stated one reason and another: it is volatile, and there is a decree lest one siphon off tar to use for something else.

lines.speaker: Story
lines.text: A cruel mother-in-law told her daughter-in-law: go anoint yourself with balsam oil, then go light the lamp. The oil caught fire and she was burned.

callout.label: Why the story here:
callout.text: It illustrates the real danger of volatile substances near open flame, motivating the Sages' extra caution with tar and similar oils.

slides.title: 🕯️ Impure Tevel — Forbidden Even on a Weekday
slides.subtitle: A verse about two kinds of teruma
slides.hebrewSource: וַאֲנִי הִנֵּה נָתַתִּי לְךָ אֶת מִשְׁמֶרֶת תְּרוּמוֹתָי
slides.label: The derivation:
slides.text: Naphtha is banned because it is volatile — but why ban ritually impure tevel, untithed produce that has not yet had teruma separated from it? The Gemara answers from Numbers 18:8, 'I have given you the charge of My terumot' — the plural teaches two terumot, pure and impure. Just as pure teruma may be used only from the moment it is actually separated, so too impure teruma may be used only from that moment. Since tevel's teruma has not yet been designated, a priest may not yet benefit from any part of it, including for light.

slides.title: 🛢️ The Tosefta's Five Opinions on Shabbat Oil
slides.subtitle: Each tanna draws the line differently
rows: May not light with tzori (balsam sap) — it is not from the tree itself
May not light with anything that comes from a tree at all
May light only with what comes from a fruit
May light only with olive oil
Objects: Babylonians have only sesame oil, Medians nut oil, Alexandrians radish oil, Cappadocians only naphtha — so nothing is forbidden except what the Sages explicitly named

callout.label: Practical result:
callout.text: Fish oil and tar are permitted; Rabbi Shimon Shezuri adds gourd oil and naphtha; Sumakhos limits animal-derived oils to fish oil alone.

nodes.content: 📜 Jeremiah 52:16 — Nebuzaradan left 'the poorest of the land' as vinedressers and husbandmen
🍇 'Vinedressers' (Rav Yosef): balsam collectors from Ein Gedi to Ramata
🐚 'Husbandmen': trappers of the ḥilazon snail, source of sky-blue dye, from Tyre's Ladder to Ḥaifa

callout.label: The point:
callout.text: Both trades yielded only a meager living for the poor, which is why they were left to work them.

slides.title: 📜 Which Fabrics Can Contract Tzaraat?
slides.subtitle: Tracing the verses from 'garment' to 'three by three'

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: only wool and linen fabric counts as a 'garment' for tzaraat impurity — other tree-based cloth does not
2️⃣ The school of Rabbi Yishmael reaches the same rule from Leviticus 13:47, which specifies wool or linen garments for the leprosy plague
3️⃣ Abaye: the two sources agree entirely. Rava disagrees — they differ over three-by-three handbreadth swatches of other fabrics
4️⃣ A baraita derives from 'the garment' (וְהַבֶּגֶד) that swatches of three-by-three fingerbreadths in wool/linen can also become impure, since warp and woof threads alone already can
5️⃣ Two exclusions in the verses ('a garment of wool or linen') teach that fabrics other than wool and linen cannot contract tzaraat impurity at all

callout.label: Bridge to next daf:
callout.text: This impurity discussion, triggered by tree-derived tzori and sukkah roofing, sets up the Gemara's next steps in defining 'garment.'

summary.principle: The Mishna's list of forbidden Shabbat-lamp fuels is grounded in real concerns — volatility, siphoning, and unseparated teruma — while a parallel discussion defines which materials count as a 'garment' subject to tzaraat impurity.

flowSteps.content: 🔥 Tar forbidden for two reasons: volatile AND feared siphoning
🕯️ Impure tevel forbidden even on weekdays — derived from 'My terumot' (plural)

columns.content: 🛢️ Tannaim dispute permitted oils; R' Yoḥanan ben Nuri: only named substances are banned
🌿 Balsam pickers and ḥilazon trappers were the era's working poor

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: A 'garment' for tzaraat impurity means wool or linen; other tree-derived fabrics are excluded

quiz.q: According to the Gemara, why is tar forbidden for lighting the Shabbat lamp?
o: Only because it smells bad
Because it is volatile and, in addition, due to a decree lest one siphon from it
Because it is too expensive
Because it is derived from an impure animal
quiz.e: The Gemara answers that two reasons were stated together: tar is volatile and potentially dangerous, and there is also a rabbinic decree lest one take sap from it.

quiz.q: Why may a priest not use ritually impure tevel for light, even during the week?
o: Because tevel is always forbidden to touch
Because the verse 'My terumot' (plural) teaches that both pure and impure teruma may be used only from the moment it is actually separated, and tevel's teruma has not been separated
Because only oil, not produce, may fuel a lamp
Because tevel is reserved exclusively for the Temple
quiz.e: Numbers 18:8 speaks of two terumot; just as pure teruma may be used only once separated, impure teruma (still part of the tevel) may not be used before it is separated.

quiz.q: How does Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri respond to a stringent list of permitted lamp oils?
o: He agrees and adds more restrictions
He notes that Babylonians, Medians, Alexandrians, and Cappadocians each have only their local oil, so nothing is forbidden except what the Sages explicitly named
He rules that only olive oil may ever be used
He says lighting is entirely optional
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri points out that different regions have access only to their local oils (sesame, nut, radish, naphtha), so the prohibition applies only to substances the Sages specifically named.

quiz.q: According to Rav Yosef, who were the 'vinedressers' left by Nebuzaradan in Jeremiah 52:16?
o: Farmers who grew grapes near Jerusalem
Balsam collectors working from Ein Gedi to Ramata
Priests who tended the Temple vineyard
Fishermen along the coast
quiz.e: Rav Yosef taught that the 'vinedressers' were the poor who collected balsam sap in the region from Ein Gedi to Ramata.

quiz.q: What is the practical difference between Abaye's and Rava's understanding of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and the school of Rabbi Yishmael?
o: Whether wool can ever become impure
Whether a three-by-three handbreadth swatch of a fabric other than wool or linen can contract tzaraat impurity
Whether linen is a valid sukkah roofing material
Whether tzori may be used for lighting
quiz.e: Rava holds the two opinions disagree specifically about three-by-three handbreadth swatches of other (non-wool, non-linen) garments becoming impure; Abaye held they were saying the same thing.
